newsitem.title: UK: Alternative origins begin competing with EU sugar.
newsitem.headline: Alternative origins begin competing with EU sugar.

text.p: Sustained demand from traditional buyers is supporting European Union (EU) sugar premiums but rising Thai and Latin American availability should start to weigh on the solid quality supply, brokers said on Friday. The main factor determining the amount of 45 ICUMSA whites available for export will be the white/raw sugar differential, although it will be unclear for some time how much tolling will be undertaken by key players such as Thailand and Mexico. The March/March premium has narrowed recently to under $70 although it is widely expected to be sold further.
"If the white market continues to drop off then obviously the Thais will think more in terms of raws," said one broker.
"But on the other hand, the more raws they produce the bigger weight there is on the market price-wise -- and the whole thing is top heavy," he said.

This week the International Sugar Organization (ISO) said Thailand should have an export availability of 4.78 million tonnes from a production of 6.63 million, close to last season's record 6.38 million.

EU premiums are already expected to come under pressure in 1997 from the new refineries in the Middle East which plan to cash in on the Gulf's huge appetite for sugar -- traditionally supplied from Europe.

The Al Khaleej refinery in Dubai aims to produce 720,000 tonnes a year and the new plant in Jeddah should turn out 500,000 tonnes. Oman also plans to set up a refinery capable of producing up to 360,000 tonnes a year.
Traders said EU premiums ex-Antwerp were quoted at a premium of $7/12 over the March LIFFE white sugar futures bid/offer for Dec/Jan shipment, while Jan/Feb cargoes were quoted at $7/10.

"European origin sugars for prompt shipment remain strong due to continuing offtake from north Africa and the Middle East," said Czarnikow Sugar in its latest monthly report, adding that the demand should continue in the run-up to Ramadan.
Syria and Tunisia have recently bought white sugar cargoes, while Iran has been a steady buyer and Iraq is said to have negotiated the purchase of 75,000 tonnes of Brazilian whites.
Recent Asian offtake has boosted premiums for Thai white sugars. Most of the crop has been sold forward for the first quarter of 1997 but should still be offered inter-trade.
"Indonesia bought a load of sugar and the trade are covering that in, Pakistan are expected to buy a lot," said another physical broker.
Traders said January/February cargoes of Thai 45 ICUMSA sugar were offered at a $20 premium, March/April bid at $8, while February and March were offered at $16 and $12.
Mexico and Brazil should dominate western hemisphere availability of white sugar into 1997, though again the precise tonnage division between whites and raws remains to be seen.
Earlier this year Mexico directly competed with the EU to supply Turkey as cargoes from Europe proved too expensive, even with its nearer geographical location.
One trade quoted prompt Mexican 45 ICUMSAs at a $10 discount to March futures and Guatemalans at a $6 discount. Similar north Braziian cargoes are still being offered but demand is said to be slack.

"North Brazils seem to be on offer but not greatly...there doesn't seem to be too much demand at all," said one trader, citing a discount of around $3 or $4 for Dec/Jan shipment. Santos 45 ICUMSA cargoes are no longer being quoted from the current crop.
